Have you ever noticed that a bowl of fruit often seems to ripen all at once? There is a simple reason for this. As many fruits ripen, they give off a gas called ethylene. The gas is invisible, but it works like a signal. When nearby fruit takes in the gas, it begins to ripen as well, and then it releases more ethylene of its own.

Ripening brings several changes. The fruit becomes softer, and its color often changes from green to yellow or red. In bananas and many other fruits, starch turns into sugar, so the fruit tastes sweeter. Bananas, tomatoes and avocados keep ripening after they are picked. Other fruits, such as grapes, strawberries and oranges, do not ripen much more once they leave the plant.

Farmers and shops make use of these facts. Bananas are usually picked while they are still green and hard, because firm fruit travels well on long journeys. Near the end of the trip, they are often kept in warm rooms with a little added ethylene, which helps them ripen evenly before they reach the shops.

You can use the same idea at home. To ripen a hard avocado faster, put it in a paper bag with a ripe banana. The bag holds the gas close to the avocado. To slow ripening down, keep ripe fruit away from other fruit, or store it somewhere cool.

Every December, our school turns the sports hall into a winter fair, and each club gets one table. Last year was the first time the woodwork club took part. There were six of us, and since September we had been carving small wooden spoons in the workshop after school. Each spoon took about three hours: sawing a rough shape from a block, hollowing the bowl with a curved knife, then sanding until the handle felt smooth. By the day of the fair we had forty of them.

We argued for a week about the price. Hugo said nobody would pay more than two dollars for a spoon, while Imogen wanted five. Our teacher, Mr Lomax, refused to help and told us to decide for ourselves. In the end we chose two dollars, wrote the price on a card and waited. The spoons were gone in less than an hour, and at first we were thrilled. Then Imogen counted the money: eighty dollars, which was barely more than we had spent on wood and sandpaper. Worse, several buyers had called the spoons cute and asked if a machine had made them.

That evening I worked it out. We had sold around a hundred and twenty hours of careful work for little more than the cost of the wood, and the low price had made people think the spoons were cheap objects rather than things made slowly by hand. Our price had told a story about the spoons, and it was the wrong story.

This year we took forty spoons to the fair again, but we did two things differently. First, we brought a log, a knife and a half-finished spoon, and took turns carving at the table while people watched. Second, we raised the price to twelve dollars and kept it there all day, with a card explaining that each spoon takes about three hours to make. I was sure we would go home with a full box.

We did not. We sold twenty-five spoons, fewer than last year, but they brought in three hundred dollars, and we used the money to buy a second set of carving knives. More surprising was the way people behaved. Instead of grabbing a spoon and walking away, they stood at the table and asked questions. An old man told us that his father had carved spoons from apple wood, and he showed us how his father used to hold the knife. Several buyers turned the spoons over in their hands for a long time before choosing one, as if the choice mattered.

Near the end of the afternoon, a girl from year seven asked if she could join the club. Mr Lomax says the real lesson of the day was about business, but I am not so sure. I think the price of a handmade thing is also a message about it. Last year our message was that the spoons were cheap toys. This year it was that someone had spent an afternoon on each one, and people listened.

In the spring of 1846, a farmer named Obadiah Raddle needed three days to haul a wagon of wheat to the market town of Rellford, a journey of only eighteen miles. The road was a strip of bare earth that turned to deep mud whenever it rained, and wagons regularly sank to their axles. Farmers in the valley could grow plenty of grain; the difficulty was getting it to buyers before it spoiled or before prices fell.

That autumn, a group of Rellford merchants led by Osmond Quarles formed a company to build something new to the region: a plank road. Workers laid two long timber beams along the route and nailed thick boards across them, side by side, like the floor of an enormous wooden hallway. The company planned to recover its costs through tolls. At gates every few miles, a keeper collected a small fee from each wagon before lifting the wooden bar that stretched across the road.

For the first few years, the road seemed a triumph. A team of horses could pull nearly twice its usual load over the smooth boards, and the trip from the valley to Rellford shrank from three days to a single day. Farmers paid the tolls without complaint, because the time they saved was worth far more than the fee. The company paid its owners generous profits, and newspapers in neighbouring districts urged their own towns to follow the example of Rellford.

The planks, however, were made of wood, and wood laid on damp ground decays. Within five years many boards had warped or split, and those resting directly on wet soil had begun to rot from beneath. Loose planks tipped up under passing wheels, and more than one horse broke a leg in a hole where a board had been. Repairs grew more frequent and more expensive each season, until they swallowed nearly all of the toll money.

The founders had made a careful estimate of what the road would cost to build, but they had treated that cost as something paid once. They had made no real plan for replacing every board within a decade, which is roughly how long the planks lasted. By 1857 the company's income had fallen below its repair bills, and its owners handed the road over to the county. Officials removed the remaining planks and spread a thick layer of gravel in their place.

It would be easy to remember the Rellford plank road simply as a failure, yet the story is more complicated. The road had shown valley farmers, for the first time, how much a dependable route to market was worth to them. When the county later asked them to pay a small yearly tax to keep the gravel road in good condition, they agreed by a wide margin. Having once travelled quickly, they were unwilling to go back to the mud.

For more than a century, the ordinary light bulb was really a small heater that happened to glow. Inside the glass, an electric current passed through a thin wire called a filament, usually made of the metal tungsten. The wire became so hot, well over two thousand degrees, that it gave off light. Yet most of the energy, roughly ninety percent, left the bulb as heat rather than as visible light. Anyone who has touched a lamp that was switched on an hour earlier has learned this quickly.

The filament also limited how long a bulb could work. At such high temperatures, tiny amounts of tungsten slowly escaped from the surface of the wire, so the filament became thinner in places until it finally broke. A typical bulb lasted about a thousand hours, which is why changing bulbs was once a regular household chore.

Light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, work in a completely different way. An LED is a tiny piece of specially prepared material, called a semiconductor, through which electricity flows. As the current moves through it, energy is released directly as light, with far less wasted as heat. An LED bulb can therefore produce the same amount of light as an old bulb while using less than a fifth of the electricity. Because there is no hot wire to wear thin, many LED bulbs are expected to last fifteen thousand hours or more.

This does not mean that LEDs stay cool. The electronics in the base of an LED bulb still produce some heat, and heat shortens their working life. For this reason, many LED bulbs have metal fins or a metal base that carries warmth away, and they may fail early if they are fitted inside a closed lamp where hot air is trapped.

The first LEDs gave off only red light, and later ones added yellow and green, which is why they were used mainly in the small indicator lights on machines. A bright white LED became practical only after engineers developed efficient blue LEDs. Most white LED bulbs today use a blue LED covered with a thin coating that changes part of the blue light into yellow. Our eyes see the mixture as white.

The change has also affected the way people shop. For decades, customers chose bulbs by their wattage, which measures how much electricity a bulb uses, and treated that number as a measure of brightness. With the old technology the shortcut worked, because a 100-watt bulb was reliably brighter than a 40-watt one. With LEDs it fails: a bulb that gives as much light as the old 60-watt type may use only eight or nine watts. Packages therefore now show lumens, a unit for the amount of light a bulb actually produces. Shoppers have had to learn to read a number that was always the real answer to their question.

passage:
In the mangrove swamps and river mouths of Southeast Asia and northern Australia lives a small fish with an unusual way of hunting. The archerfish feeds partly on insects that rest on leaves and twigs above the water. Instead of leaping for them, it knocks them down by shooting a thin jet of water from its mouth. A well-aimed shot can hit an insect resting a metre or more above the surface, and the stunned insect drops into the water, where the fish quickly swallows it.

The fish has no special water gun inside its body. It presses its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth, forming a narrow tube, and then snaps its gill covers shut. This squeezes water forward through the tube at high speed. When researchers filmed the jets with high-speed cameras, they noticed something surprising: the back of the jet travels faster than the front. As the jet moves through the air, the rear water catches up with the leading water, so that much of it gathers into one heavy drop near the target.

Aiming is a harder problem than it first appears. Light bends as it passes between air and water, so an insect seen from below the surface appears to be in a slightly different place from where it really is. A human spear fisher standing in a stream must learn to aim below the spot where a fish appears to be. The archerfish faces the same puzzle from the other side of the surface, yet it hits targets from many different angles. Experiments suggest that it does not simply line up with the image it sees; instead, it appears to correct for the bending of light, much as an experienced spear fisher does.

Young archerfish are not born expert shooters. They improve with practice, but laboratory studies suggest they can also improve by watching. In one kind of experiment, young fish were allowed to observe a skilled fish hitting targets that moved across a screen above the tank. Afterwards, many of the watchers hit moving targets far better than before, even though they had barely practised on such targets themselves. Many scientists had once assumed that learning by observation of this kind was limited to animals with large brains, such as apes and some birds.

Hunting is also a race. When an insect falls, other fish nearby rush toward it, so the shooter must reach the landing point first. Within roughly a tenth of a second after the insect starts to fall, the archerfish turns and swims toward the place where it will land. It judges this from the insect's early speed, direction and height, rather than waiting to see where it drops.

Taken together, these findings have made the archerfish a favourite subject for scientists who study how animals think. A single hunt combines physics, careful aim, learning and fast prediction. The fish suggests that such skills can develop in an animal whose brain is small and built very differently from our own.

Three hundred years ago, the main street of Hallowmere looked very different from today. Above almost every shop door hung a painted wooden sign with a picture on it. A baker showed a loaf of bread, a shoemaker showed a boot, and a locksmith showed a large golden key. These pictures rarely changed, and a shop often kept the same sign for a hundred years, even after a new family took it over.

The pictures had a practical purpose. Many people in the town could not read, so a written name over the door would have helped only a few customers. A picture could be understood by everyone, including farmers who came in from nearby villages on market day.

The signs also worked as addresses. Houses had no numbers yet, so people gave directions by naming the pictures. A letter might be sent to the tailor beside the green hen, and the messenger would know exactly where to go.

Over time, however, the signs became a problem. Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones, and some stretched halfway across the street. They blocked light from upper windows and creaked loudly in the wind. In 1771, after a heavy sign fell and injured a horse, the town council ordered that every sign be fixed flat against the wall. Later, when the town began to number its houses, many shops replaced their pictures with painted names.
